adamant.overview: A hard substance, whether composed of diamond, some other gemstone, or some type of metal.

wiki_secs.t: Adamant in classical mythology is an archaic form of diamond. The English word diamond is ultimately derived from adamas, via Late Latin diamas and Old French diamant. In ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adamas), genitive ἀδάμαντος (adamantos), literally 'unconquerable, untameable'. In those days, the qualities of hard metal (probably steel) were attributed to it, and adamant became an independent concept as a result.

In the Middle Ages adamant also became confused with the magnetic rock lodestone, and a folk etymology connected it with the Latin adamare, 'to love or be attached to'. Another connection was the belief that adamant (the diamond definition) could block the effects of a magnet. This was addressed in chapter III of Pseudodoxia Epidemica, for instance.

Since the contemporary word diamond is now used for the hardest gemstone, the increasingly archaic noun adamant has been reduced to mostly poetic or anachronistic use. In that capacity, the name, and various derivatives of it, are frequently used in modern media to refer to a variety of fictional substances.

In Greek mythology, Cronus castrated his father Uranus using an adamant sickle given to him by his mother Gaia. An adamantine sickle or sword was also used by the hero Perseus to decapitate the Gorgon Medusa while she slept.

as-sirat.overview: A narrow bridge which every person must pass on the Yawm ad-Din ("Day of the Way of Life" i.e. Day of Judgment) to enter Paradise.

wiki_secs.t: As-Sirāt (Arabic: الصراط) is, according to Islam, the bridge over which every person must pass on the Yawm al-Qiyamah (lit. 'Day of Resurrection') in order to enter Jannah (lit. 'Paradise').

It is not explicitly mentioned in the Quran, but described in the Hadith. As-Sirāt is said to be thinner than a strand of hair and as sharp as the sharpest knife or sword (because of its danger). Below this path are the fires of Hell, which burn the sinners to make them fall. Those who performed acts of goodness in their lives are transported across the path at speeds according to their deeds leading them to the Hawd al-Kawthar (lit. 'Pond of Abundance').

On Judgement Day, after the dead have been resurrected, assembled, and judged by God, the saved and the damned now being clearly distinguished, the souls will traverse over hellfire via the bridge of As-Sirāt. The faithful will "move easily and swiftly across a broad path", led first of all by Muhammad and other leading lights of the community on their way to Jannah;  those judged guilty of sin but still considered to be mu'minun (lit. 'believers') will fall from the bridge into jahannam (lit. 'hellfire') but remain there only for a limited period of purgation; unbelievers, however, will find the bridge has become "sharper than a sword and thinner than a hair" and darkness blinds their way. Their inevitable fall from the bridge will be an "inescapable descent" into their fiery destination of everlasting punishment.

wiki_secs.t: Bear worship (also known as arctolatry) is a form of animal worship and is the religious practice of worshipping bears. Bears are often viewed as ancestors or spiritual messengers by those who practice arctolatry. The practice can involve both the reverence and ritual slaughter of bears. Archaeologists have debated the advent of the ceremonial treatment of bear remains, but some evidence suggests the practice may date back to the Middle Paleolithic in Neanderthal populations. Bear worship is a common practice across many circumpolar northern cultures. The practice is associated with bear remains and can be traced back geographically to North Eurasian populations, including the Ainu, Nivkh, Sámi, Finno-Ugric, and other Siberian peoples.

Bear worship is sometimes referred to as "arctolatry." The term arctolatry combines two distinct linguistic roots. The prefix "arcto-" comes from the Ancient Greek word "arktos," meaning "bear," which itself shares a root with the Proto-Indo-European word for bear. The suffix "-latry" comes from the Greek word "latreia," meaning "worship" or "service," stemming from latris, meaning "servant" or "worshipper."

The existence of an ancient bear cult among Neanderthals in Western Eurasia during the Middle Paleolithic has been a subject of debate in the archaeological community. Some archaeologists suggest that the bear was considered a primeval god and the she-bear a mother goddess. Some archaeologists have suggested that Neanderthals worshipped the cave bear (Ursus spelaeus). Ancient bear bones have been discovered in several caves. The earliest representation of bears in a cave was found in the Eastern Pyrenees.

During excavations, some on-site archaeologists try to determine whether the bones were arranged in a way that could only have resulted from direct intervention rather than natural deposition. Some archaeologists, such as Roger Constant, consider this evidence of a bear cult that originated during the Paleolithic period. Constant has defended the idea of a bear cult and played a role in the reintroduction of live bears near a discovery site.

crown-of-thorns.overview: According to the New Testament, a woven crown of thorns (Ancient Greek: στέφανος ἐξ ἀκανθῶν, romanized: stephanos ex akanthōn or ἀκάνθινος στέφανος, akanthinos stephanos) was placed on the head of Jesus during the events leading up to his crucifixion. It was one of the instruments of the Passion, employed by Jesus' captors both to cause him pain and to mock his claim of authority. It is mentioned in the gospels of Matthew (Matthew 27:29), Mark (Mark 15:17) and John (John 19:2, 19:5), and is often alluded to by the early Church Fathers, such as Clement of Alexandria, Origen and others, along with being referenced in the apocryphal Gospel of Peter.

gae-bulg.overview: The Gáe Bulg (Old Irish pronunciation: [ɡaːi̯ ˈbulg]) (also Gáe Bulga, Gáe Bolg, Gáe Bolga), meaning "spear of mortal pain/death", "gapped/notched spear", or "belly spear", was the name of the spear of Cú Chulainn in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology. article.html:
No object in European legend has meant so much while being described so little. Chrétien de Troyes gives the Grail a few lines: a maiden, a light that outshines the candles, a dish of gold and jewels. He never says what it is for, and that silence is the point. Perceval, the boy who asks too many questions, has learned to keep quiet, and so the one question that matters goes unasked. The Grail begins as a test of attention.

Every writer after Chrétien tried to fill the silence. Robert de Boron filled it with sacred history, making the dish the cup of the Last Supper and the blood of Christ. Wolfram filled it with a mysterious stone and a brotherhood of knights. The authors of the Queste filled it with theology, and their Grail could be seen only by the pure. Each answer reveals what its age most wanted: grace, wonder, purity, a reason for knighthood.

The Grail is also a story about a wound. The Fisher King cannot heal, and his land lies waste. The question Perceval fails to ask is not "what is it?" but "whom does it serve?": a question about relation rather than possession. That is why the Grail has been so easily borrowed by psychologists, poets and pilgrims alike. It is a vessel, and a vessel is defined by what it holds.

In the modern world the Grail has become almost anything sought and never found: the cure, the code, the treasure, the bloodline, the perfect wave. The comedy of Monty Python works because the quest is so recognisable: earnest men wandering through a confusing country, looking for something they could not describe if they found it. Behind the jokes the old shape remains. Someone is wounded, a land is dry, and the right question, asked with compassion, might still make it green.

For a writer, the Grail's most useful lesson may be its first one: an object becomes powerful by being withheld. Chrétien showed it once and never explained it, and eight centuries of storytellers have been answering him ever since.

debates.html:
The oldest texts are French and Christian, yet the story's wounded king, waste land and food-giving vessel look older.

  • Celtic origin. Held by Roger Sherman Loomis and, before him, Alfred Nutt: the Grail descends from Irish and Welsh magic vessels of plenty and rebirth, like the Dagda's cauldron or the cauldron of Annwn, passed to French poets by Breton storytellers.loomis
  • A Christian, literary creation. Held by Richard Barber and many recent scholars: no Celtic text has a grail; Chrétien invented a mystery and his successors gave it meaning, in an age of intense devotion to the Eucharist.barber
  • A ritual survival. Held by Jessie Weston: the remains of a fertility cult. Now largely abandoned.weston
  • Steppe origins. Held by C. Scott Littleton and Linda Malcor (From Scythia to Camelot, 1994): Sarmatian and Alan traditions, carried west by soldiers in the Roman army, including a magic cup in the Ossetian Nart sagas. A minority view.wp

• Valencia's Holy Chalice. An agate cup that some archaeologists date to around the first century BCE or CE, set in a medieval mount. Venerated, and used by two popes, though the Church has never declared it the cup of the Last Supper.valencia
  • Other claimants. The Sacro Catino of Genoa (once thought to be emerald), the Chalice of Doña Urraca in León (named the Grail in a 2014 book, a claim most historians reject) and the wooden Nanteos Cup in Wales, said to heal.wp
  • None of them. Most historians see the Grail as a literary object first, with relics attached to it later.barber

lifetime.html: There is no grail in antiquity, but its ingredients are old. The Gospels tell of the cup Jesus shared at the Last Supper (Matthew 26:27–28) and of Joseph of Arimathea, who buried him (Matthew 27:57–60). Irish and Welsh tradition knew magic vessels of plenty and rebirth, like the Dagda's cauldron, which some scholars see as the Grail's ancestors.biblewp

The Grail is a creation of the decades around 1200: Chrétien (c. 1180–1191), his continuators, Robert de Boron, Wolfram, the Perlesvaus and the Welsh Peredur. The great prose Vulgate Cycle (c. 1215–1235) gave it its classic form in the Quest of the Holy Grail: Galahad, son of Lancelot, achieves it, with Perceval and Bors, and the Grail is taken up to heaven. Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, printed by Caxton in 1485, carried this "Sangreal" into English.questemalorywp

After the Reformation the romances fell out of fashion, but cups said to be the Grail were venerated as relics. The agate cup in Valencia Cathedral, the Santo Cáliz, was given to the cathedral in 1437 by King Alfonso V of Aragon; Genoa kept the green glass Sacro Catino, long believed to be carved from a single emerald.valenciawp

The nineteenth century revived it: Tennyson's poem "The Holy Grail" (1869) in Idylls of the King, and Wagner's last opera, Parsifal (1882). Jessie Weston's From Ritual to Romance (1920) read it as the relic of a fertility rite and gave T. S. Eliot the frame for The Waste Land (1922). In the twentieth century it became a vessel for psychology, occult theories, conspiracy and comedy, and "holy grail" came to mean any ultimate goal.idyllswestonwp

myth.html:
The grail enters literature in Chrétien de Troyes's unfinished romance Perceval, the Story of the Grail, written around 1180–1191 for Philip, Count of Flanders. The young knight Perceval, guest of a wounded king who fishes because he cannot ride, watches a procession pass: a youth with a white lance whose point bleeds, then a maiden carrying un graal, a wide dish shining with gems, then a silver platter. Taught not to talk too much, Perceval asks nothing. Next morning the castle is empty, and he learns that one question (whom does the grail serve?) would have healed the king and his land.chretienwp

Chrétien says a grail, not the Grail: in Old French a graal was a broad serving dish. Later in the poem a hermit explains that it carries a single Mass wafer that has kept the Fisher King's father alive for years, and calls it "so holy a thing". The poem breaks off before Perceval returns, which invited a crowd of continuators to finish it.chretienhelinandwp

Within a decade or two Robert de Boron, in Joseph of Arimathea, gave the vessel a Christian history: it was the dish or cup of the Last Supper, in which Joseph of Arimathea caught the blood of the crucified Christ; Joseph's family carried it west, to the "vales of Avaron". Robert built on the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, which had already enlarged Joseph's role. From then on the Grail was holy.boronwp

In Wolfram von Eschenbach's German Parzival (c. 1200–1210) it is not a cup at all but a stone, the lapsit exillis, kept by knights at the castle of Munsalvaesche and renewed each Good Friday by a wafer brought by a dove. In the Welsh Peredur the procession carries a severed head on a platter.wolframperedurwp

overview.html: A mysterious vessel at the heart of the Arthurian legends: first a nameless serving dish carried through a hall in a twelfth-century French romance, within a generation the cup of the Last Supper that caught Christ's blood, and ever since the object of a quest that only the purest knight can finish.chretienboronwp

seen.html: For the authors of the Queste del Saint Graal the Grail is the grace of God made visible, above all in the Eucharist. Worldly chivalry fails before it; only Galahad, chaste and humble, sees it openly. Scholars often trace the Queste's severe spirituality to Cistercian monks.questebarber

Wolfram's Grail is a stone that feeds its keepers and chooses its own servants, and his Parzival wins it through compassion and growth rather than purity alone. Joseph Campbell, in Creative Mythology (1968), read Wolfram's poem as the first great myth of the individual seeking his own path.wolframcampbell

Tennyson's knights ride off after a vision most of them cannot see, and the Round Table falls apart: the quest is holy, but it also pulls them away from the duties that keep the realm alive. Wagner made the Grail the centre of a drama of suffering redeemed by compassion.idyllswp

Jessie Weston argued that the wounded king, the waste land and the vessel and lance were the remains of a pre-Christian fertility cult, in which the health of the land depends on the health of the king. Few scholars hold this now, but it shaped modernist literature.weston

Emma Jung and Marie-Louise von Franz, in The Grail Legend (1960), read the vessel as an image of the Self, the wholeness the psyche seeks, and Perceval's failure to ask as a failure of consciousness.jungvf

hrotti.overview: Norse mythology contains references to various named weapons wielded by specific characters. The oldest references sometimes offer nothing except a name for the weapon, but some of them include more detail on the weapon and what makes it unique, such as Thor's famous hammer Mjölnir. These weapons have often been expanded upon in later cultural adaptations that involve Norse mythology. For example, Richard Wagner's Ring cycle of operas adds that Wotan (Odin)'s spear Gungnir is inscribed with all the agreements and treaties which Wotan has made with various other beings, and is the record and source of his power.

love-potion.overview: A love potion (poculum amatorium) is a magical liquid which supposedly causes the drinker to develop feelings of love towards the person who served it. Another common term to describe the potion, philtre, is thought to have originated from the ancient Greek term philtron ('love charm'), via the French word philtre. The love potion motif occurs in literature, mainly in fairy tales, and in paintings, drama, music and mythology. In the Middle Ages, extracts from nightshades were used as hallucinogens, and to make supposed love potions and flying ointments.

throne.overview: A throne is the seat of state of a potentate or dignitary, especially the seat occupied by a sovereign (or viceroy) on state occasions; or the seat occupied by a pope or bishop on ceremonial occasions. "Throne" in an abstract sense can also refer to the monarchy itself, an instance of metonymy, and is also used in many expressions such as "the power behind the throne". A throne is a symbol of divine and secular rule and the establishment of a throne as a defining sign of the claim to power and authority. It can be with a high backrest and feature heraldic animals or other decorations as adornment and as a sign of power and strength. A throne can be placed underneath a canopy or baldachin.

uaithne.overview: In Irish mythology, Uaithne (Old Irish: Úaithne, pronounced [ˈuənʲə]) is Dagda's harp, or rather the Dagda's harper, according to a number of modern translators (cf. § Attestations).
uaithne.list_note: The harp which belongs to The Dagda. After the Second Battle of Mag Tuired the Fomorians had taken The Dagda's harp with them. The Dagda found it in a feasting-house wherein Bres and his father Elathan were also. The Dagda had bound the music so that it would not sound until he would call to it. After he called to it, it sprang from the wall, came to the Dagda and killed nine men on its way.

veil-of-veronica.overview: The Veil of Veronica, or Sudarium (Latin for sweat-cloth), also known as the Vernicle, the Veronica and the Holy Face, is a Christian relic consisting of a piece of cloth said to bear an image of the Holy Face of Jesus produced by miraculous means (an acheiropoieton). Various existing images have been claimed to be the original relic or an early copy of it; representations of it are also known as vernicles. The story of the image's origin is related to the sixth Station of the Cross, wherein Saint Veronica, encountering Jesus along the Via Dolorosa to Calvary, wipes the blood and sweat from his face with her veil. was-sceptre.overview: The was (Egyptian wꜣs "power, dominion") or uas sceptre is a symbol that appeared often in relics, art, and hieroglyphs associated with the ancient Egyptian religion. It appears as a stylized animal head at the top of a long, straight staff with a forked end. Was sceptres were used as symbols of power or dominion, and were associated with ancient Egyptian deities such as Set or Anubis as well as with the pharaoh. Was sceptres also represent the Set animal or Khnum. In later use, it was a symbol of control over the force of chaos that Set represented.

"Sir," saith the Knight, "He that would go before the Saviour of the World ought of right to apparel him as fairly as he may.  I am by confession purged of all wickedness and of all the misdeeds that ever I have committed, and do repent me truly thereof, wherefore at this moment am I fain to die."

"Sir, my Lady sendeth for him and beseecheth him by me, for the sake of the Saviour of the World, that if he had ever pity of dame or damsel, he will take vengeance on Nabigant that hath slain her men and destroyed her land, for she hath been told how he that won back the Golden Circlet ought of right to take vengeance upon him."

Now, in _Macbeth_ also the Weird Sisters are described as “black.” The coming up of Hekate with them in the cave-scene might not unfitly be looked upon as a parallel with the German Held, or Rach-Hel, and the Norse Hel; these Teutonic deities being originally Goddesses of Nocturnal Darkness, and of the Nether World, even as Hekate.
